item.content:encoded:
Key Takeaways
- Anxious attachment can cause difficulty trusting others, a need for reassurance, and anxiety when away from a partner.
- Self-awareness and clear communication can help people with anxious attachment build healthier relationships.
- A licensed therapist can offer strategies for coping and communicating.
You know the feeling—the one you get after finally hitting send on that well-crafted text to your new love interest, and an hour goes by, then two, then 10, and they still haven’t replied? The way your mind jumps to the conclusion that they aren’t interested in you anymore, or that they can’t text you because they are hanging out with someone else—even if things have been going great? If this sounds familiar, it’ll give you a sense of what it’s like dating while living with an anxious attachment style.
“Anxiously attached people are hungry for connection and will also be apprehensive of its reliability,” says Sabrina Romanoff, PsyD. “They tend to amplify emotional signals as they seek evidence of other people’s responsiveness to them.”
What Is Anxious Attachment?
According to attachment theory, first proposed by British psychologist John Bowlby and later expanded by Mary Ainsworth, a person’s attachment style usually develops in childhood through interactions with a primary caregiver.
An anxious attachment style arises during childhood when parents are present and then suddenly absent, whether physically or emotionally. If someone doesn’t receive adequate emotional responsiveness as a child, they may become skeptical of dependability in adulthood.
Kelsey, 32
I went through a string of codependent relationships before learning I had an anxious attachment style. I was abandoned as a child, and the evidence of that trauma has historically been very apparent in my romantic relationships.
Several traits characteristic of this attachment style can show up in both emotions and behaviors.
“In adults, it manifests through the desire for intimacy while also experiencing difficulty trusting others, fear of emotional closeness, difficulty with boundaries, need for consistent reassurance, a tendency to be obsessive or clingy, or the experience of anxiety when away from one’s partner,” says Romanoff.
Anxious attachment can also develop from early dating experiences. If someone cheated on you or you had multiple instances of rejection in your teens or early twenties, it could have a significant impact on how you connect with future partners.
How Can Symptoms Show Up In Dating?
Olivia, 27, shares, “I learned I have an anxious attachment style when I was dating someone and realized my heart rate would increase whenever his phone dinged, whenever he mentioned hanging out with another female, and whenever he would go work out at a certain place.”
Digital communication can be a real trigger for anxious types as well. Madeline, 29, shares how texting can provoke feelings of insecurity: “My anxious thoughts tend to spiral when I’m not with the guy I’m dating. When we’re together, I usually feel fine because I have the reassurance that they want to spend time with me, so most of my anxiety happens with texting.”
Madeline continues, “There was one time I was panicking over a boy not texting me to confirm the brunch plans we were supposed to have the next day. I let my friend write him a text, but she sent it without my approval, and I nearly had a heart attack. Looking back, I was being so irrational. And that guy was someone that I didn’t even want to be my boyfriend. But I cared so much about making him like me.”
Because anxiously attached individuals have a fervent need for acceptance, it can easily lead to chronic people-pleasing behaviors. This can have real consequences for mental health when the fear of rejection overpowers the ability to love yourself or recognize your own needs.
Erica, 41
My patterns of people-pleasing extended to the point of self-abandonment, for the sake of avoiding suffering my partner’s anger or contempt. I never acknowledged my own needs (or even knew that I had any); I exhausted myself emotionally and physically to offer as much of myself as possible, and never reciprocated the criticism that was dealt to me.
How Does It Affect Relationships?
Anxious feelings can come up at every stage of a relationship, no matter how stable it is. These factors can add stress to someone’s dating life.
“When it comes to romantic relationships, people with anxious attachment desire connection and love. However, at the same time, they find it difficult to trust people, creating overwhelming insecurity about their relationships,” says Yalda Safai, MD. “As a result, behaviors such as jealousy, possessiveness, and constant need for reassurance become common in these individuals.”
These feelings of suspicion and doubt can seriously strain a relationship. It usually doesn’t matter how many times the anxious partner is validated. Deep down, they’ll still anticipate abandonment, and even be attracted to signs of it.
Related Stories
One of the best-known books on attachment theory, “Attached,” by Rachel S.F. Heller and Amir Levine, explains that anxiously attached individuals are often drawn to people with an avoidant attachment style.
This may seem counterintuitive, but the idea is that when an anxious person is innately wired to expect their partner to treat them poorly, they are subconsciously attracted to individuals who can’t truly show up in the relationship. What’s worse, an anxious person will work extra hard to convince an avoidant partner to stay with them, which inevitably leads to them being treated poorly. It’s a vicious cycle.
Madeline, 29
I tend to date guys that don’t want to spend every night together, but then I get anxious that they don’t want to spend enough time with me. Then I spiral into thinking they don’t like me, they’re planning to dump me, etc.
When these feelings go unchecked, it can put a ton of undue pressure on the other partner and, in many cases, unintentionally push them away. A huge part of a healthy relationship is trusting that your partner loves you and has your back, but constant doubt can be a catalyst for decline.
Take the Attachment Style Quiz
If you’re unsure about your attachment style, this fast and free quiz can help you identify what your thoughts and behaviors may say about your attachment.
How Modern Dating Habits Can Contribute to Anxiety
Attachment theory is a buzzy concept these days, and for good reason: It can help you understand how you behave in relationships and relate to your partners. That said, if you find this article relatable, it doesn’t necessarily mean you’re anxiously attached.
The realities of modern dating can make every interaction anxiety-provoking. Insecurity is the name of the game because no one wants to commit when it feels like someone better is always one swipe away. We’ve normalized ghosting, the slow fade, poor communication skills, and a lack of clarity around relationships—all things that can make anyone wary about putting themselves out there.
And if you do, in fact, have an anxious attachment style, dating apps can provide that quick fix of attention and validation, allowing you to avoid facing the perpetual insecurity that causes the craving for praise in the first place. Every new match or compliment provides a little dopamine boost, which reinforces the cycle.
There is nothing wrong with you if you’re anxiously attached, but cultivating awareness will help you feel more grounded and confident in your romantic pursuits.
How To Build Healthier Relationships
Self-awareness and communication are key to addressing the thoughts and reactions caused by an anxious-attachment style.
“In order to form healthy relationships, it is important to, first of all, become aware of your attachment style,” says Safai. “Second, learning how to express your emotions is extremely important for any individual and, in particular, those who suffer from an anxious attachment personality style.”
It may also be helpful to date someone with a secure attachment style. “It can help you understand what a stable and secure relationship is like,” says Safai. It may also encourage you to break possible patterns of dating avoidant individuals who could be reinforcing your expectations of abandonment.
Kelsey, 32
Recently, I’ve been working toward viewing conflict as a means to understanding my partner and learning how to support him instead of listening to the inner narrative that frames conflict as a threat to my relationship... Yoga, therapy, and a lot of breathwork have been very healing and incredibly helpful in my ability to feel safe within myself and less reliant on those I’m in a relationship with
“There is a healthy balance between recognizing when reassurance seeking is excessive and effectively asking to get your needs met by your partner,” says Romanoff. “The reality is, you are more likely to find safety in a relationship if you are aware of your needs and explicitly share with your partner how to make you feel secure.”
When To Seek Care
If you’re prone to insecurity in your relationships, there is nothing wrong with you, but it helps to understand how it influences the way you relate to others. In today’s complex dating scene and beyond, we can all benefit from tips and tricks for managing anxious attachment.
If you suspect you may have this attachment style, it’ll help to talk to a licensed therapist. They can offer strategies for coping and communication when intense emotions might be giving you a warped view of your partner’s behavior.
